newsitem.title: USA: GM says Canada strike won't affect UAW talks.
newsitem.headline: GM says Canada strike won't affect UAW talks.

text.p: General Motors Corp said Wednesday the possibility of a strike in Canada will not affect the automaker's U.S. bargaining with the United Auto Workers union.

GM spokesman Gerry Holmes said company and UAW negotiators continued to make progress on Wednesday and do not intend to slow their pace if the Canadian Auto Workers strike GM's Oshawa, Ontario, and Ste. Therese, Quebec, plants at midnight.
"We're working pretty much independently," Holmes said of negotiations in the United States and Canada. "I don't think we're waiting for one or the other" to strike a deal first.

He declined to confirm reports that GM was near an agreement with the UAW for a new national labor contract covering some 215,000 hourly workers. "We're continuing to make progress, and both us and the UAW are working to try to reach a conclusion," he said.
Union sources said the two sides were still at odds over the issues of GM's ability to shift work to outside suppliers -- known as outsourcing -- and employment guarantees.

The contract signed by Ford Motor Co, which is being used by the UAW as a pattern for the industry, guarantees jobs for about 95 percent of the automaker's 105,000 hourly UAW workers. On Sunday, Chrysler Corp signed a largely similar agreement, which will be considered by the automaker's plant-level UAW leaders on Thursday.

Although the guarantee provisions are designed to discourage outsourcing, sources familiar with the Ford contract say it allows the automaker to eliminate some jobs that are made unnecessary by changes in technology and by productivity gains.
That provision would greatly help GM, which is introducing a number of new vehicles over the next several years that will require fewer workers to assemble them.

But the automaker still has up to 14 parts plants that it considers "troubled," and it remains unclear whether the UAW will allow GM to sell them or will help make them competitive. GM makes more of its own parts than Ford and Chrysler do.
In Canada, CAW president Buzz Hargrove has steadfastly resisted GM's plans to sell two Ontario parts plants and shift other work to outside suppliers.
Some UAW officials said they disagree with Hargrove's willingness to wage a strike over outsourcing.

"Hargrove over in Canada, he's taking a barbaric position that they can't sell the plants," said Bob Sykes, financial secretary for UAW Local 14 at GM's transmission plant in Toledo, Ohio. "You can't let them be stuck with uncompetitive operations when the other companies are buying their parts on the outside."
Sykes said GM cannot guarantee union jobs if it signs a contract that forces it to remain uncompetitive.
